## Recall...
\framesubtitle{Conditions for validity of inference in linear regression}


 - The relationship between $X$ and $Y$, if there is one, is actually \textbf{L}inear
   - e.g. not quadratic, exponential, etc.

\vspace{2mm}

 - \underline{\textbf{I}ndependence of observations}

\vspace{2mm}

 - \textbf{N}ormality of $\epsilon_i$
   - Note that this can also be achieved, due to the central limit theorem, with a large sample size even if $\epsilon_i$ does not follow a normal distribution

\vspace{2mm}

 - \textbf{E}qual variance across all values of $X$
   - Also known as homoskedasticity
   
   
## Time Series Data {.t}

Simply put, time series data are data that are collected over time.

Time Series data violate the independence condition because measurements at various time points may be dependent.

::: {.t}
### Examples:
\vspace{-2mm}
 - Stock market prices over days, hours, minutes or seconds
 - Temperature in San Diego over days or years
 - Quiz scores within individual students over days or weeks
 - Consumer spending, vehicle traffic over weekdays or weekends
 - Blood glucose over minutes or months
:::

**Important**: Time scale matters


## Time Series Data {.t}
\framesubtitle{Example: Luteinizing hormone} 

Luteinizing hormone (LH) is a hormone produced by the pituitary gland at the base of the brain that regulates the reproductive system.

The \texttt{lh} data consists of 48 measurements of LH every 10 minutes.

```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, size="footnotesize", fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
data(lh)
print(lh)
```


## Time Series Data {.t}
\framesubtitle{Example: Luteinizing hormone} 

```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, size="footnotesize", fig.width=5, fig.height=3, echo = FALSE}
plot(lh, main = "Luteinizing Hormone Levels", ylab = "Level", xlab = "Time (10-min intervals)")
```

There seems to be some temporal dependence.


## Time Series Data {.t}
\framesubtitle{Independent normals}

What would the data look like if time points were independent?

```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, size="footnotesize", fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
mu = mean(lh); sigma = sd(lh); n = length(lh)
y.iid = ts(rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma))
plot(y.iid, main = "iid data", ylab = "Level", xlab = "Time (10-min intervals)")
```



## Time Series Data {.t}
\framesubtitle{Example: Luteinizing hormone} 

Check temporal dependence: plot $y_t$ against $y_{t-1}$

```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, size="footnotesize", fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
plot(lh[2:n] ~ lh[1:(n-1)], main = "Luteinizing Hormone Levels", ylab = "lh[2:n]", xlab = "lh[1:(n-1)]", pch = 16)
```


## Time Series Data {.t}
\framesubtitle{Independent normals}

Check temporal dependence: plot $y_t$ against $y_{t-1}$

```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, size="footnotesize", fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
plot(y.iid[2:n] ~ y.iid[1:(n-1)], main = "iid data", ylab = "y.iid[2:n]", xlab = "y.iid[1:(n-1)]", pch = 16)
```


## Time Series Data {.t}
\framesubtitle{Example: Luteinizing hormone} 

Let's center the data and fit a linear model:

\vspace{5mm}
```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, size="footnotesize", fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
lh.c <- lh - mean(lh)
model1.lh <- lm(lh.c[2:n] ~ lh.c[1:(n-1)] - 1)
round(summary(model1.lh)$coefficients, 4)
```


## Time Series Data {.t}
\framesubtitle{Example: Luteinizing hormone} 

```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, size="footnotesize", fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
plot(lh.c[2:n] ~ lh.c[1:(n-1)], main = "Luteinizing Hormone Levels", ylab = "lh.c[2:n]", xlab = "lh.c[1:(n-1)]", pch = 16)
abline(model1.lh, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```


## Time Series Data {.t}
\framesubtitle{Independent normals} 

Compare to the iid normals:

\vspace{5mm}
```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, size="footnotesize", fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
y.iid.c <- y.iid - mean(y.iid)
model1.iid <- lm(y.iid.c[2:n] ~ y.iid.c[1:(n-1)] - 1)
round(summary(model1.iid)$coefficients, 4)
```


## Time Series Data {.t}
\framesubtitle{Independent normals} 

Compare to the iid normals:

```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, size="footnotesize", fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
plot(y.iid.c[2:n] ~ y.iid.c[1:(n-1)], main = "Luteinizing Hormone Levels", ylab = "y.iid.c[2:n]", xlab = "y.iid.c[1:(n-1)]", pch = 16)
abline(model1.iid, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
```


## AR(1) Model {.t} 

A time series autoregressive model of order 1, denoted AR(1), is:
$$
y_t = \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \epsilon_t, \qquad \epsilon_t \sim \text{iid } N(0, \sigma^2)
$$
Note that there is **no intercept**.

The data need to be *centered* before fitting the model (that is, subtract the mean).

What would happen if we added an intercept?
$$
y_t = \phi_0 + \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \epsilon_t
$$


## AR(1) Model {.t} 
\framesubtitle{Parameter restrictions}

https://www.abcwebsites.online/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/quickpoll-cloud.html#

Are there any restrictions on the parameter $\phi_1$?

A. No restrictions

B. $\phi_1$ must always be non-negative

C. $\phi_1$ must be less than 1

D. $|\phi_1|$ must be less than 1

## AR($p$) Model {.t} 

We can add more predictors as time points from the past.

An autoregressive model of order $p$ is denoted AR($p$):
$$
y_t = \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \phi_2 y_{t-2} + \cdots + \phi_p y_{t-p} + \epsilon_t
$$


## AR($p$) Model {.t} 
\framesubtitle{Lynx trappings}

The \texttt{lynx} dataset describes annual Canadian lynx trappings in the years 1821–1934.

```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, size="footnotesize", fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
data(lynx)
plot(lynx)
```


## AR($p$) Model {.t} 
\framesubtitle{Lynx trappings}

The data looks skewed:

```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, size="footnotesize", fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
hist(lynx, breaks = 10)
```

All values are positive: these are counts.


## AR($p$) Model {.t} 
\framesubtitle{Lynx trappings}

We can improve it with a log transformation

```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, size="footnotesize", fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
y <- log10(lynx)
hist(y, breaks = 10)
```


## AR($p$) Model {.t} 
\framesubtitle{Lynx trappings}

Now the time series looks like this:

```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, size="footnotesize", fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
plot(y)
```


## AR($p$) Model {.t} 
\framesubtitle{Lynx trappings}

Try an AR(1) model:

```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, size="footnotesize"}
y.c <- y - mean(y)
n <- length(y.c)
model1.y <- lm(y.c[2:n] ~ y.c[1:(n-1)] - 1)
round(summary(model1.y)$coefficients, 4)
```
\vspace{5mm}
Try an AR(2) model:

```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, size="footnotesize"}
model2.y <- lm(y.c[3:n] ~ y.c[2:(n-1)] + y.c[1:(n-2)] - 1)
round(summary(model2.y)$coefficients, 4)
```


## AR($p$) Model {.t} 
\framesubtitle{Lynx trappings}

Try an AR(3) model:

```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, size="footnotesize"}
model3.y <- lm(y.c[4:n] ~ y.c[3:(n-1)] + y.c[2:(n-2)] + y.c[1:(n-3)] - 1)
round(summary(model3.y)$coefficients, 4)
```

\vspace{5mm}
And an AR(4) model:

```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE, size="footnotesize"}
model4.y <- lm(y.c[5:n] ~ y.c[4:(n-1)] + y.c[3:(n-2)] + y.c[2:(n-3)] + y.c[1:(n-4)] - 1)
round(summary(model4.y)$coefficients, 4)
```


## Two types of time series models {.t}

::: {.t}
### An AR($p$) model:
\vspace{-6mm}
$$
y_t = \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \phi_2 y_{t-2} + \cdots + \phi_p y_{t-p} + \epsilon_t
$$
:::

(see Lab 9 for more details)


\vspace{7mm}

::: {.t}
### An MA($q$) model: 
\vspace{-6mm}
$$
y_t = \epsilon_t + \theta_1 \epsilon_{t-1} + \theta_2 \epsilon_{t-2} + \cdots + \theta_q \epsilon_{t-q}
$$
:::

where each $\epsilon_i$ is independently $N(0, \sigma^2)$.

\vspace{3mm}

Let's break this one down a little here...


## AR(p) vs. MA(q) models {.t}
\framesubtitle{But first: what is the difference between these two?}
For simplicity, let's consider AR(1) vs. MA(1).

::: {.t}
### AR(1)
\vspace{-7mm}
$$
y_t = \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \epsilon_t
$$
:::

::: {.t}
### MA(1)
\vspace{-7mm}
$$
y_t = \epsilon_t + \theta_1 \epsilon_{t-1}
$$
:::

Key difference: 

 - In the AR(1) model, even though $y_t$ only explicitly depends on $y_{t-1}$, it is also true that $y_{t-1}$ depended on $y_{t-2}$, and so on. So, impacts last longer than just the value of $p$.
 - Conversely, in the MA(1) model, $y_t$ depends on $y_{t-1}$ only through its error term. So, impacts only last the length of $q$.



## MA(q) models {.t}

Again, suppose $q=1$. Then, an MA(1) model would be:

$$
y_t = \epsilon_t + \theta_1 \epsilon_{t-1}
$$

So as a simple example, suppose $\theta_1=1, \sigma=1$. Then $\epsilon_1$ and $\epsilon_0$ are both independently $N(0, 1)$ so,

```{r}
set.seed(1)
eps0 <- rnorm(n=1, mean=0, sd=1)
eps1 <- rnorm(n=1, mean=0, sd=1)
eps0
eps1
```

## MA(q) models {.t}
Now,
```{r, echo=FALSE}
eps <- rnorm(5)
```

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_1 &= \epsilon_1 + \epsilon_0 = `r eps1` + `r eps0` = `r eps1 + eps0` \\
y_2 &= \epsilon_2 + \epsilon_1 = `r eps[1]` + `r eps1` = `r eps[1] + eps1` \\
y_3 &= \epsilon_3 + \epsilon_2 = `r eps[2]` + `r eps[1]` = `r eps[2] + eps[1]` \\
y_4 &= \epsilon_4 + \epsilon_3 = `r eps[3]` + `r eps[2]` = `r eps[3] + eps[2]` \\
y_5 &= \epsilon_5 + \epsilon_4 = `r eps[4]` + `r eps[3]` = `r eps[4] + eps[3]` \\
y_6 &= \epsilon_6 + \epsilon_5 = `r eps[5]` + `r eps[4]` = `r eps[5] + eps[4]` \\
\end{aligned}
$$

ok but what is actually happening here?

## MA(q) models {.t}
Comparing the MA(1) model to a simple independent N(0, 1) model:

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="90%"}
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)
set.seed(1)
theme_update(text=element_text(size=20))
x <- 1:100
y1 <- rnorm(101) # 1 extra for "burn-in"
y2 <- NULL
for(i in 1:100){
  y2[i] <- y1[i+1] + y1[i]
}

dat1 <- data.frame(x=x, y1=y1[2:101])
dat2 <- data.frame(x=x, y2=y2)

p1 <- ggplot(data=dat1, aes(x=x, y=y1)) + geom_line() + labs(title="Independent N(0,1)")
p2 <- ggplot(data=dat2, aes(x=x, y=y2)) + geom_line() + labs(title="MA(1)")

grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol=1)
```

## MA(q) models {.t}
\label{macode}
Here's the code that made the plot on the previous slide:

```{r, eval=FALSE, size="footnotesize"}
library(ggplot2)
library(gridExtra)
set.seed(1)
theme_update(text=element_text(size=20))
x <- 1:100
y1 <- rnorm(101) # 1 extra for "burn-in"
y2 <- NULL
for(i in 1:100){
  y2[i] <- y1[i+1] + y1[i]
}

dat1 <- data.frame(x=x, y1=y1[2:101])
dat2 <- data.frame(x=x, y2=y2)

p1 <- ggplot(data=dat1, aes(x=x, y=y1)) + geom_line() + 
  labs(title="Independent N(0,1)")
p2 <- ggplot(data=dat2, aes(x=x, y=y2)) + geom_line() + 
  labs(title="MA(1)")

grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol=1)
```


## MA(1) model vs. AR(1) model {.t}
Let's quickly go back and compare...

::: {.t}
### In the MA(1) model we had:
\vspace{-6mm}
$$
\begin{aligned}
y_1 &= \epsilon_1 + \epsilon_0  \\
y_2 &= \epsilon_2 + \epsilon_1  \\
y_3 &= \epsilon_3 + \epsilon_2 \\
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: {.t}
### Conversely, in the AR(1) model,
\vspace{-2mm}
with $\phi_1=1$ and suppose $y_0=0$, it would be:
$$
\begin{aligned}
y_1 &= y_0 + \epsilon_1 = \epsilon_1 \\
y_2 &= y_1 + \epsilon_2 = y_0 + \epsilon_1 + \epsilon_2 \\
y_3 &= y_2 + \epsilon_3 = y_0 + \epsilon_1 + \epsilon_2 + \epsilon_3 \\
\end{aligned}
$$
:::


## MA(q) models {.t}
Now comparing the MA(2) model to a independent N(0, 1) model:

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="90%"}
y1 <- c(y1, rnorm(1))
y3 <- NULL
for(i in 1:100){
  y3[i] <- y1[i+2] + y1[i+1] + y1[i]
}

dat1 <- data.frame(x=x, y1=y1[3:102])
dat2 <- data.frame(x=x, y3=y3)

p1 <- ggplot(data=dat1, aes(x=x, y=y1)) + geom_line() + labs(title="Independent N(0,1)")
p2 <- ggplot(data=dat2, aes(x=x, y=y3)) + geom_line() + labs(title="MA(2)")

grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol=1)
```
